> AURA is a compact, custom hardware controller powered by a Raspberry Pi Pico that brings physical controls to developer workflows. Equipped with an EC11 rotary encoder and a 0.96" SSD1306 OLED screen, AURA operates as an air-gapped USB HID device. It allows you to scrub line-by-line through source code in VS Code, step cleanly through debugger execution breakpoints, and navigate Git commit diffs without moving your hands away from your workstation or physical study materials. ### 2026-10-11 – # Complete Hardware Design & Firmware Architecture

**13h**

# Complete Hardware Design & Firmware Architecture

Over the course of designing **AURA**, I built a custom mechanical macro pad  to optimize my navigation and media control. Instead of relying on generic macro pads, I wanted a fully custom board featuring a Raspberry Pi Pico, an SSD1306 OLED display for media metadata, an EC11 rotary encoder for scrolling and volume control, and 6 mechanical keys.

Here is the complete log of the work completed across the design phases:

## 1. Schematic Design & Pin Mapping (`eeschema`)
* **Microcontroller:** Integrated the Raspberry Pi Pico (`RaspberryPi_Pico_Debug`) as the brain of the board.
* **OLED Display:** Wired an SSD1306 OLED screen via I2C, mapping Pico `GPIO0` (I2C0 SDA) and `GPIO1` (I2C0 SCL).
* **Rotary Encoder:** Connected an EC11 encoder (`GPIO14` and `GPIO15` for rotation pulses, and `GPIO16` for the built-in push switch).
* **Macro Keys & Mounting:** Scaled the design from an initial 3-key layout up to a full **6-key mechanical matrix** (`SW2` through `SW7`) tied to `GPIO02` through `GPIO07` with common ground paths. Added **4 M3 mounting holes** (`H1`–`H4`) in the corners for a secure enclosure build.
* **Rule Checks:** Applied No-Connect flags (`X`) to all unused pins and successfully passed the Electrical Rules Check (ERC).

## 2. PCB Layout & Copper Pour
* **Component Placement:** Arranged the switches in a clean, ergonomic grid layout maintaining standard 1u (19.05 mm) spacing, positioned the OLED and encoder neatly above, and placed the Pico on the left side.
* **Routing & DRC Constraints:** Routed all signal traces on the front and back copper layers, resolving track width and constraint rules to clear all Design Rules Checker (DRC) errors.

## 3. Firmware Architecture (CircuitPython & USB HID)
* **HID Emulation:** Designed the `code.py` script to utilize CircuitPython's `adafruit_hid` library, allowing the macro pad to act as a standard USB keyboard and consumer control device.
* **Dynamic Configuration:** Implemented a `config.json` file loader on the `CIRCUITPY` drive, enabling keybindings to be easily customized without recompiling code.
* **Encoder Modes:** Programmed multi-function encoder behavior—normal rotation handles vertical scrolling, `Shift + rotation` handles horizontal scrubbing, and `Fn + rotation` controls system volume.
* **OLED Metadata & Sleep Mode:** Configured real-time display tracking for song titles, artist info, and progress bars, along with an automatic 15-minute inactivity sleep timer to dim the display.

### 2026-10-22 – Today I spent 2 hours working on **AURA**, focusing on two major milestones: optimizing the PCB layout to cut down manufacturing costs, and then jumping into OpenSCAD to design the custom 3D-printable

**2h**

Today I spent 2 hours working on **AURA**, focusing on two major milestones: optimizing the PCB layout to cut down manufacturing costs, and then jumping into OpenSCAD to design the custom 3D-printable case!

### 1. Tightening up the PCB layout in KiCad
When looking at the initial board dimensions, I realized there was a bit too much wasted space between the switches, the Raspberry Pi Pico, and the OLED display. Since PCB fabrication costs scale with overall board size, reducing the footprint was a top priority.
* Moved Cherry MX switches closer together.
* Re-routed the traces for the EC11 rotary encoder and the 0.91" OLED display.
* Kept the four corner mounting holes locked in place for structural stability.

![Screenshot 2026-10-22 191542](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/MqfXtqzyoV3kC5NbjDzdPoc1zza7pyWb/909bcc8fd745873cda24ce61c67f6c7474342bd497c66ef86f8a7702054377ef.png)
### 2. Moving on to Enclosure Design
With the board geometry finalized, my next goal was to build a clean 3D-printable case using OpenSCAD. Designing an enclosure around a custom board can be tricky with clearances—you need just enough tolerance so the PCB slips in smoothly without rattling around.

![Screenshot 2026-10-22 191505](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/MqfXtqzyoV3kC5NbjDzdPoc1zza7pyWb/7e617fae9a524549760db41d431c79f8c9d89aae01a8f2b00d0fad3cea9af453.png)

Getting the coordinate math right for the internal standoffs and walls took a few iterations, but it's coming together nicely! Next session, I'll finish up the top lid geometry and the bottom half of the case and assemble the exclosure with the PCB into 1 .step file

**Total time spent: 2h**

### 2026-10-23 – Today I spent 2 hours diving deep into **Fusion360 and Onshape** to design a custom 3D-printable enclosure for the AURA.

**4h**

Today I spent 2 hours diving deep into **Fusion360 and Onshape** to design a custom 3D-printable enclosure for the AURA.

Designing a case around a custom PCB always sounds straightforward until you start dealing with tight tolerances and coordinate math. My main goal for this session was to build a clean two-part enclosure complete with internal mounting standoffs and precise cutouts for the Raspberry Pi Pico USB port, the OLED display, and the rotary knob.

### Tackling PCB Coordinates & Properly Uploading the Assembled Model of the PCB

One of the trickiest parts of making this enclosure was making sure that the PCB and all the components on that PCB come together perfectly so that I can just make the enclosure on it.

![Screenshot 2026-10-23 224855](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/MqfXtqzyoV3kC5NbjDzdPoc1zza7pyWb/a207b924eff3c12304c3361afcdf79c3d07069d8aee8153e9f44c9ed70206732.png)

But somehow it got the PCB in a proper and assembled way

![Screenshot 2026-10-22 191505](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/MqfXtqzyoV3kC5NbjDzdPoc1zza7pyWb/7e617fae9a524549760db41d431c79f8c9d89aae01a8f2b00d0fad3cea9af453.png)

### Making the enclosure around it

After I got the issue out of the way, I started to design the enclosure with the PCB as the reference and made a simple box.

Then after much more sketching, extruding, shelling, and much more things, I finally got the final AURA enclosure ready, which actually fits the PCB with enough tolerance to easily fit inside it.

The base has 1 cutout on the back, which lets us plug the power/data connector to the Raspberry Pi Pico.

The lid has the cutouts for the screen, the knob, and the 6 switches so that I can easily access them.

![Screenshot 2026-10-22 214441](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/MqfXtqzyoV3kC5NbjDzdPoc1zza7pyWb/24191a7828613564c08307d69ca6d9dabe9c11b4d3d351768f6b2fd4ed3a2d65.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-22 214454](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/MqfXtqzyoV3kC5NbjDzdPoc1zza7pyWb/5aed7384cdcbda76be1ad26d5d31567db8d3af370bddf3e051da470cc58012d4.png)

(The color of the base and the lid will be black only, so I kept the base in the default color and changed the top to distinguish it from the base, making the work easier.)

### Bringing all the things to one place

After the enclosure was finished, I exported the base, the lid, and the fully assembled step. (The full step file contains both the base and the lid assembled together assembled with the PCB inside of it.)

I have also updated the BOM for the new price of the PCB and the 3D printing.

**Total time spent: 4h**
